title: Plot, Setting and Theme
bigQuestion: How does a story about particular people in a particular place end up saying something true about everyone?

story.title: The Argument About the Sunset
story.kicker: Two readers, one novel, one sunset, and a disagreement that turned out to be the whole point of the book.
paragraphs: Two eighth graders in a Chicago classroom were arguing, quietly, because the teacher was nearby. They had both finished The Outsiders. Jada said the book was about a gang fight and some boys who ran away. Miguel said it was about the sunset. Jada laughed at him. "A sunset is a sunset," she said. "He looks at the sky. It's a nice sky. Move on."

Miguel opened the book to the scene where Ponyboy, a poor greaser, talks with Cherry Valance, a rich Soc, outside a drive-in. Ponyboy tells her he watches sunsets. Cherry says she watches them too, from her side of town. Miguel pointed at the page. "Same sunset. Different sides of town. The whole book is right there." Jada read it twice and did not say anything for a while.

Then she went looking. She found the sunset again near the end, in the note Johnny leaves for Ponyboy, where he talks about staying gold and about how Ponyboy can still see sunsets like a kid does. She found a poem in the middle of the book, by Robert Frost, about how the first green of spring is gold and does not last. She found that every time the sunset came back, somebody had lost something.

By the end of the period, Jada had changed her mind, but not all the way. "Fine," she said. "The sunset means something. But the book is still about the fight. The fight is what happens. The sunset is what it means." Miguel thought about that and decided she was right. They had discovered, without the words for it yet, the difference between plot and theme.

This chapter gives you those words. Plot is what happens, in what order, and why one thing leads to the next. Setting is where and when it happens, and why the where matters. Theme is what the story says about people, the part that stays true when you close the book. Symbols, like a sunset, are how a writer gets from one to the other without preaching. You will learn to find all of them and to prove what you find.
story.think: Jada said the fight is what happens and the sunset is what it means. Can a story have what happens without what it means? Can it have meaning without events?

lessons.title: Five Parts of a Plot
lessons.mainIdea: Most plots move through exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution, and naming those parts helps you see how a story is built.
reading: A girl moves to a new town and knows nobody. She joins the track team and gets faster. A rival on the team starts sabotaging her. On the day of the championship, she has to decide whether to run or to report the rival and miss the race. She runs, and wins, and reports the rival afterward. In the last scene she is eating pizza with three new friends. You just read a whole plot, and it has five parts.

The *exposition* sets things up: who, where, and what is normal. The girl is new and alone. The *rising action* is the chain of events that builds tension: the team, the speed, the sabotage. Each event makes the next one more likely, and the stakes go up. The *climax* is the moment of highest tension, where the main character faces the central choice or conflict head on: run or report.

The *falling action* shows the results of the climax playing out: she wins and reports. The *resolution* shows the new normal: pizza with friends. Some stories skip or shrink a part. A short story might have one line of exposition. A mystery might put the climax on the last page and give you almost no falling action. But the shape is there under most stories, and once you see it, you can predict where a book is headed.

In The Outsiders, the exposition is Ponyboy's walk home and the fight, plus what he tells you about his brothers and friends. The rising action runs from the drive-in through the park. The night in the park, and the flight to the church, push the story toward its climax. Readers argue about exactly which scene is the climax, the fire or the rumble or the hospital, and that argument is a good one to have with evidence.

words.d: the opening part of a plot that introduces characters, setting, and the normal situation
the series of events that build tension toward the climax
the turning point of highest tension, where the main conflict comes to a head
the events after the climax that show its results
the ending, where conflicts are settled and a new normal is shown

look.title: Sentences per Plot Part
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the track story in the first paragraph
look.prompt: In this tiny story, the rising action gets the most sentences. In a full novel, which part usually takes the most pages, and why?

check.q: Which part of the plot introduces the characters and the normal situation?
check.why: Exposition sets up who, where, and what is normal before the tension builds.

check.q: In the track story, which event is the climax?
choices: The girl moves to a new town
The girl must decide whether to run or report the rival
The girl eats pizza with friends
The girl joins the track team
check.why: The climax is the moment of highest tension where the main choice must be made.

check.q: What is the job of rising action?
choices: To show the new normal at the end
To build tension through a chain of events that raise the stakes
check.why: Rising action is the chain of events that increases tension toward the climax.

lessons.title: Why the Climax Comes Late
lessons.mainIdea: Writers place the climax near the end and build to it so that the resolution feels earned, and the placement shapes how a reader feels.
reading: Imagine a story where the big fight happens in chapter two and the next twelve chapters are cleanup. You would put it down. Now imagine the fight comes in chapter thirteen of fourteen, after every chapter has made it harder to avoid. You cannot put it down. Same fight. Different place. Where a writer puts the *climax* controls how a reader feels for the whole book.

The rising action is supposed to make the climax feel necessary. Each event should close off an easier choice. In The Outsiders, the greasers and Socs could have kept their distance. Then a fight in a park goes wrong, and hiding becomes impossible, and a church fire turns the boys into something the town has to look at. By the time of the rumble, nobody can back out. That is the feeling of rising action done well: the walls closing in.

After the climax, the falling action and resolution are usually short, but they are not filler. They tell you what the climax cost and what it changed. A story that ends the moment the fight ends leaves you hanging. A story that shows the day after, quietly, tells you what the fight was for. The last chapters of The Outsiders are mostly Ponyboy trying to get up in the morning, and that is the point.

When you read, mark the page where you think the climax is. Then check it two ways. Was everything before it building pressure? Is everything after it release? If yes, you found it. If the pressure keeps building after your mark, you were early. Being early is not a mistake. It means the writer fooled you on purpose, and that is worth noticing too.

words.d: what a character stands to win or lose; higher stakes mean more tension
the feeling of worry or suspense a reader has while waiting to see what happens

look.title: Two Versions of One Story
look.text: Version A: Chapter 1, the twins find the map. Chapter 2, they find the treasure. Chapters 3 through 10, they spend it. Version B: Chapters 1 through 9, the twins search, lose the map, fight, and get it back. Chapter 10, they dig.
look.prompt: Which version would you rather read, and what does your answer tell you about where a climax belongs?

check.q: Why do writers usually place the climax near the end?
choices: So the reader can skip to it
So the tension has time to build and the ending feels earned
Because the climax is the least important part
check.why: A late climax gives the rising action room to close off easy choices and raise the stakes.

check.q: What should the events of rising action do to the main character's choices?
choices: Close off easier options until the conflict must be faced
check.why: Good rising action removes escape routes so the climax feels necessary.

check.q: What do the falling action and resolution tell a reader?
choices: What the climax cost and what it changed
check.why: The ending shows the results and meaning of the climax rather than just stopping.

lessons.title: Subplots
lessons.mainIdea: A subplot is a smaller story running beside the main one, and it usually reflects or pushes the main plot.
reading: The main story is about a boy trying to get his family through a hard year. Beside it, in a few scenes a chapter, is a smaller story about his sister learning to drive. The driving lessons never become the main event. But they show the same family under less pressure, and the day she finally passes her test is the day the boy first believes things might turn out. The small story is a *subplot*.

A subplot is a second, smaller plot woven through the main one. It has its own beginning, rise, and end. Writers use subplots for several reasons. A subplot can give the reader a break from the main tension. It can develop a minor character. Most importantly, it can echo the main plot's theme from a different angle, or cross into the main plot and change it.

In The Outsiders, the friendship between Ponyboy and Cherry Valance is a subplot. It does not drive the fights. But every time it appears, it shows that a greaser and a Soc can talk like people, which is what the main plot keeps saying is impossible. Sodapop's troubles with his girlfriend are another subplot, and they come crashing into the main story when Ponyboy and Darry's arguing finally becomes too much for him.

To find a subplot, look for a thread of scenes about a different problem than the main one, with its own little arc. Then ask what it is doing there. If it echoes the main plot, name the echo. If it crosses into the main plot, mark the crossing. A subplot that does neither may just be padding, and readers are allowed to say so.

words.d: a smaller story that runs alongside the main plot and usually reflects or affects it
a series of connected scenes about one problem or relationship running through a book

look.title: Spotting the Echo
look.text: Main plot: Kenji is trying to save a failing community garden before the city sells the lot. Subplot: Kenji's grandfather, who has stopped speaking since Grandma died, starts coming to the garden and, one morning, tells Kenji the name of a tomato plant.
look.prompt: How does the grandfather subplot echo the main plot? What might happen if the two threads cross?

check.q: What is a subplot?
choices: The climax of the main plot
A smaller story that runs beside the main plot
check.why: A subplot is a second, smaller story with its own arc that runs alongside the main plot.

check.q: In The Outsiders, what does the Ponyboy and Cherry subplot show?
choices: That a greaser and a Soc can talk like people
That the rumble was Cherry's idea
check.why: Their friendship echoes the theme that the two groups are not as different as the town believes.

check.q: Which is a fair test of whether a subplot belongs in a book?
choices: Whether it is longer than the main plot
Whether it has a happy ending
Whether it is about the narrator
Whether it echoes the main plot or crosses into it
check.why: A good subplot reflects or affects the main story. One that does neither may be padding.

lessons.title: Flashback and Foreshadowing
lessons.mainIdea: Flashback jumps backward to show earlier events; foreshadowing plants hints about events to come.
reading: Halfway through a scene at a funeral, the narrator says, "The last time I saw her laugh was the summer we painted the fence," and suddenly you are at the fence, three years earlier, paint on your hands. Then you are back at the funeral. The story jumped in time. That jump is a *flashback*, and it lets a writer show the past instead of just summarizing it.

Writers use flashback when the past explains the present. A character's fear of water makes sense once you see the day at the lake. The clue that the story is jumping is usually a change of verb tense, a line like "years before," or a sense memory that pulls the narrator back. When you notice one, ask what the writer needs you to see now that you could not have understood earlier.

*Foreshadowing* works the other way. It plants a hint about something that has not happened yet. A character mentions that the old bridge is unsafe. Nobody crosses it for a hundred pages. When someone finally does, you feel a chill because you were warned. Foreshadowing can be a line of dialogue, an object, a bit of weather, or even a title. It is often only visible the second time you read.

In The Outsiders, Ponyboy's early remark that he wishes he looked tougher foreshadows how much his looks and his innocence will matter. Johnny's carrying a knife after he was beaten foreshadows the park. On a first read, these are details. On a second read, they are the writer telling you exactly what is coming, if you are paying attention.

words.d: a scene that interrupts the story to show something that happened earlier
a hint or clue placed early in a story about something that will happen later
the form of a verb that shows when something happens, such as past or present

look.title: A Hint in the First Paragraph
look.text: The ice on the pond was thick enough, everyone said, if you stayed near the edge. Tomas nodded and did not mention that the middle was where the fish were.
look.prompt: What is being foreshadowed? Which words do the work? How would you feel if Tomas appeared with a fishing pole in chapter four?

check.q: A scene interrupts the present action to show what happened three years earlier. This is:
check.why: A jump backward in time to show an earlier event is a flashback.

check.q: Why do writers use flashback rather than just summarizing the past?
choices: It lets readers see the past scene and feel it, not just hear about it
It hides the past from the reader
check.why: Showing a scene gives readers the experience, which is stronger than a summary.

check.q: Which is the best example of foreshadowing?
choices: A character remembers her first day of school
The narrator explains the town's history
A character says the old bridge is unsafe, and much later someone crosses it
check.why: An early hint that pays off later is foreshadowing.

lessons.title: Setting That Does Work
lessons.mainIdea: Setting is when and where a story happens, and in good writing it shapes characters, creates conflict, and builds mood.
reading: Take a story about two friends who fall out and set it in a Chicago apartment in January, with the radiators clanking and nobody able to go outside. Now set the same story in a wide, empty field in June. The words the friends say could be identical, but the stories are not. In the first, they are trapped together. In the second, one can walk away. The *setting* changed what the fight can be.

Setting is the time and place of a story: the year, the season, the hour, the city, the room. Weak writing treats it as a backdrop, a painted wall behind the actors. Strong writing makes it do work. Setting can shape characters, because a boy raised in a town that sorts people by money grows up thinking that is normal. Setting can create conflict, because a blizzard or a border or a curfew is a force to fight against.

Setting also builds *mood*, the feeling a reader gets from a scene. A writer chooses details on purpose: a dripping faucet, a streetlight buzzing, a hallway that smells like floor cleaner. Each one tunes the reader's nerves. When you notice a writer spending a paragraph on a place, ask what feeling the details are building and what that feeling is for.

The Outsiders never names its city, but its setting is precise: a mid-1960s American town with an east side and a west side, drive-in theaters, vacant lots for fights, and an abandoned church in the countryside. The east-west line is the whole conflict. The church, far from town, is the one place a greaser and a Soc could not be told apart, which is exactly what the boys learn there.

words.d: the time and place in which a story happens, including season, hour, and specific locations
the feeling a piece of writing creates in the reader, such as dread, calm, or loneliness

look.title: Same Fight, Two Rooms
look.text: A: The radiator knocked twice and went silent. Snow leaned against the window. Dee sat on the far end of the couch, which was not very far. B: The field ran to the tree line. Dee stood up, brushed off her jeans, and could have been a mile away in a minute.
look.prompt: Which details build mood in each version? In which version is the coming argument more dangerous, and why?

check.q: What is setting?
choices: The main conflict of a story
The time and place in which a story happens
check.why: Setting is the when and where, from the era down to the specific room.

check.q: In the two-friends example, how did setting change the story?
choices: It changed whether the friends were trapped together or free to leave
check.why: The winter apartment traps them; the open field lets one walk away. Setting changed the conflict.

check.q: Why does the abandoned church matter as a setting in The Outsiders?
choices: It is where the rumble happens
It is far from the town's east-west divide, so the boys are not sorted there
It is on the west side
check.why: Away from town, the social line disappears, which lets the boys see themselves differently.

lessons.title: Theme, Topic and Moral
lessons.mainIdea: A topic is what a story is about in a word; a theme is what it says about that topic in a sentence; a moral is a lesson it orders you to follow.
reading: Ask three students what The Outsiders is about. One says "friendship." One says "people on both sides of a divide have the same fears and the same sky." One says "don't judge people by their money." All three are pointing at something real, but they are pointing at three different things: a topic, a theme, and a moral.

A *topic* is a subject, usually one or two words: friendship, class, loss, growing up. A topic is not yet an idea. A *theme* is what the story says about the topic, and it takes a full sentence: "Loyalty to friends can cost more than it gives." A theme is an insight about people or life that the story shows to be true, and a strong novel has more than one.

A *moral* is a direct lesson or rule, the kind that ends a fable: be honest, work hard, do not judge. Fables have morals. Most novels do not. A novel with a moral tends to feel like a lecture. A novel with a theme trusts you to think. The difference is that a theme describes how the world is, and a moral tells you what to do about it.

When you write a theme, avoid two mistakes. Do not stop at the topic: "The book is about class" is a start, not a theme. Do not name the characters: "Ponyboy learns that Socs have problems too" is a plot summary. A theme leaves the characters behind and says something that could be true outside the book: "People who seem to have everything can still be hurting."

words.d: the subject of a story in a word or two, such as friendship or loss
an insight about people or life that a story shows to be true, stated as a full sentence
a direct lesson or rule that a story teaches, common in fables

look.title: Sort the Three
look.text: About one short story, three readers wrote: (1) Courage. (2) Always stand up to bullies. (3) Being brave often means being scared and acting anyway. One is a topic, one is a moral, one is a theme.
look.prompt: Which is which? Rewrite the moral as a theme, and turn the topic into a theme of your own.

check.q: Which of these is a theme rather than a topic or a moral?
choices: Family can be the people who choose to stay, not only the people you are born to
check.why: A theme is a full-sentence insight about life that reaches beyond the characters.

check.q: What is the difference between a theme and a moral?
choices: A theme describes how the world is; a moral tells you what to do
A moral is only found in novels
check.why: Themes are insights; morals are instructions. Fables have morals; most novels have themes.

check.q: Why is 'Ponyboy learns that Socs have problems too' not a good theme statement?
choices: It names the characters, so it is plot summary rather than an idea about life
check.why: A theme should be true outside the book, so it should not depend on the characters' names.

lessons.title: How a Theme Grows
lessons.mainIdea: Theme is not stated once; it develops across a whole text through repeated situations, changing characters, and the ending.
reading: A theme is not hiding in one sentence you can underline. It grows. Early in a book a situation comes up. Later it comes up again, a little different. A character reacts one way the first time and another way the last time. The ending tips the balance. By the last page, the book has made an argument without ever stating it, and you have to put it into words yourself.

The best way to watch a theme grow is to follow one *pattern*: a repeated situation, image, or question. In The Outsiders, the pattern is people looking at each other across a line. Greasers look at Socs and see money. Socs look at greasers and see trouble. Then Cherry talks to Ponyboy. Then a Soc named Randy tells Ponyboy he is tired of the fighting. Each time the pattern returns, the line gets a little thinner.

Character change is the second way theme develops. When a *dynamic* character ends up believing something new, the book is usually asking you to consider believing it too. Ponyboy's shift from "they have it easy" to "things are rough all over" is the theme walking on two legs. If you can describe the change, you can state the theme.

The ending is the last word. A story that ends with a reunion says something different from one that ends with a funeral, even if everything before was the same. When you write about theme, use all three sources: the pattern, the change, and the ending. A theme with evidence from all three is hard to argue with.

words.d: a situation, image, or question that repeats through a text, often carrying its theme
to grow and become clearer over time, as a theme does across a whole text

look.title: One Pattern Across a Model Story
look.unit: scenes where a character crosses a line they were told not to
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a nine-chapter model story written for it
look.prompt: The pattern peaks in chapter 7 and nearly vanishes in chapter 9. What might have happened in the story to make crossing the line stop mattering?

check.q: Which is the best description of how theme works in a novel?
choices: It is stated in one sentence in chapter one
It develops across the text through patterns, character change, and the ending
It is the same as the plot
It is only found in the title
check.why: Theme grows through repeated situations, changing characters, and how things end.

check.q: In The Outsiders, what repeated pattern carries the theme?
choices: Characters looking at each other across a social line
check.why: The book keeps returning to greasers and Socs seeing each other, and the line thins each time.

check.q: Two stories are identical except one ends with a reunion and one with a funeral. What is true?
choices: The endings give them different themes
check.why: The ending is the last word on what a story says, so different endings mean different themes.

lessons.title: Symbols and Motifs
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a thing in a story that stands for a larger idea; a motif is a repeated element that builds meaning; both need evidence, not guesswork.
reading: A sunset is light hitting the atmosphere at a low angle. In The Outsiders it is also the one thing a greaser and a Soc can share, and a sign of the innocence Johnny begs Ponyboy to keep. When a concrete thing in a story carries a larger meaning, it is a *symbol*. The sunset does not stop being a sunset. It becomes a sunset and something more.

Writers signal symbols by repetition and by placement. A thing that appears once is probably just a thing. A thing that appears at the beginning, at a turning point, and at the end, and that characters talk about, is asking to be read. The gold in Frost's poem, which Ponyboy recites in the church, links up with the sunset and with Johnny's last words, and together they make one symbol out of three pieces.

A *motif* is a repeated element, like an image, a phrase, or a sound, that builds meaning over a text. Motifs are broader than symbols. In The Outsiders, hair is a motif: the greasers' long hair is their pride and their label, and cutting it in the church is a real loss. A motif may not stand for one idea the way a symbol does, but it keeps a theme in front of you.

Be careful. Not everything means something, and readers who insist that every blue curtain stands for sadness get things wrong. Test a symbol the way you test any inference: find the repetitions, find the placement, find a character or narrator who treats it as important, and state what it stands for in the book's own terms. If you cannot find that evidence, it is a curtain.

words.d: a concrete thing in a story that also stands for a larger idea
an image, phrase, or element that repeats through a text and builds meaning
the state of not yet knowing the world's harm; freshness of seeing

look.title: The Poem in the Church
look.text: Nature's first green is gold, / Her hardest hue to hold.
look.cite: Robert Frost, "Nothing Gold Can Stay," 1923 (the poem Ponyboy recites in The Outsiders)
look.prompt: Gold here is not metal. What is it? How does the poem's idea of gold connect to the sunset and to Johnny's note?

check.q: What is a symbol in literature?
choices: A word that is spelled with capital letters
A concrete thing that also stands for a larger idea
check.why: A symbol is a real object, place, or image in the story that carries added meaning.

check.q: What is the best evidence that something in a story is a symbol?
choices: It repeats at key moments and characters treat it as important
check.why: Repetition, placement at turning points, and characters' attention signal a symbol.

check.q: How does a motif differ from a symbol?
choices: A motif is a repeated element that builds meaning; a symbol stands for a specific larger idea
A motif is always a color
check.why: Motifs repeat and keep a theme in view; symbols stand for something specific.

lessons.title: The Book and the Movie
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing a novel to its film shows what each form can and cannot do, and every change a filmmaker makes is a choice worth explaining.
reading: In 1983 the director Francis Ford Coppola made The Outsiders into a movie with a cast of young actors who later became famous. Students who read the book and then watch the film usually notice the same things. The movie looks right: the hair, the cars, the lot. But something is missing. Ponyboy's thoughts, which fill every page, are mostly gone, because a camera cannot film a thought.

That is the first thing a comparison teaches: the two forms have different tools. A novel can go inside a mind. It can stretch a moment across three pages or skip a year in a sentence. A film has faces, music, light, and sound, and it can make you feel a sunset in one shot that took the book a paragraph. Neither is better. Each has to do the other's work in its own way.

The second thing to learn is that every change is a choice. Filmmakers cut scenes for time, add scenes for clarity, and move things around for pace. When you notice a difference, do not just say the movie left it out. Ask what the change does. Does it make a character simpler? Does it lose a subplot that carried a theme? Does it make the ending happier or sadder than the book's? The original release of The Outsiders film trimmed the story's beginning and end, and a later, longer edition restored some of those scenes.

To write a comparison, pick one scene that both versions include. Describe exactly what each does with it. Then argue which version served the theme better and why. That is a fair fight, and it teaches you more about the book than praising or bashing the movie ever could.

words.d: a work changed from one form to another, such as a novel made into a film
the speed at which a story moves; films and books control it with different tools

look.title: What the Camera Cannot Do
look.text: In the novel, Ponyboy spends a paragraph after the fight describing how tough he wishes he looked, how he feels about his brothers, and why he does not like to be touched. In the film, the same moment is a boy on the sidewalk with a cut on his face, and the camera holds on him for three seconds.
look.prompt: What did the film lose and what did it gain? What could an actor do in three seconds to carry some of what the paragraph said?

check.q: Why do readers of The Outsiders often feel something is missing from the film?
choices: The film changes the setting to a big city
Ponyboy's inner thoughts, which fill the book, cannot be filmed directly
check.why: A novel goes inside a mind; a camera shows only what can be seen and heard.

check.q: What is the most useful question to ask about a difference between a book and its film?
choices: What does the change do to characters or theme?
check.why: Every change is a choice, and the effect of the change is what matters in a comparison.

check.q: Which is a fair method for writing a book-versus-film comparison?
choices: Listing every scene the film cut
Saying which one you liked more
Choosing one shared scene and arguing which version served the theme better
check.why: A focused, evidence-based comparison of one scene teaches more than a list or a preference.

lessons.title: Writing About Theme
lessons.mainIdea: A strong theme paragraph states the theme as a sentence, supports it with specific evidence from the text, and explains how the evidence shows the theme.
reading: Here is a weak paragraph about theme: "The theme of The Outsiders is that people are the same. Ponyboy learns this. It is a good lesson." It names a topic, not a theme. It has no evidence. It ends with an opinion. A teacher reading it cannot tell whether the writer read the book. Here is how to fix it, step by step.

First, state the theme as a full sentence about life, not about the characters: "People divided by money and class often share the same fears and the same losses." Second, give specific evidence from the text. Not "Cherry and Ponyboy talk," but the sunset exchange at the drive-in, where Cherry says she watches the same sunset from her side of town. Add a second piece: Randy, a Soc, telling Ponyboy he is sick of the fighting.

Third, explain the link. "Both moments show a Soc admitting to a greaser something the town says they cannot share. The sunset is the same sky over both neighborhoods, and Randy's exhaustion is the same fear both sides feel. The book puts these scenes at its center to show that the line between the groups is drawn by money, not by what people actually feel."

Finally, deal with the other side. A strong paragraph admits what might argue against the theme, such as the fact that the fighting does not stop, and answers it: the book does not claim the line disappears, only that it is not real in the way the boys believed. Claim, evidence, reasoning, and an honest look at the other side. That is a paragraph a teacher can trust.

words.d: the explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it
a point that seems to argue against your claim, which a strong writer names and answers

look.title: A Theme Paragraph, Marked
look.text: CLAIM: Loyalty can ask more of a person than fairness would. EVIDENCE: In the model story, Ana lies to the principal to protect her brother even though she knows he broke the window. REASONING: She chooses her brother over the truth and pays for it with a suspension, which shows the cost the story is weighing. OTHER SIDE: Some readers say she was just afraid. But she says herself that she would do it again.
look.prompt: Find the four parts. Which part would you cut if you had to, and what would the paragraph lose?

check.q: What is wrong with 'The theme of The Outsiders is that people are the same'?
choices: It is a topic-like statement with no evidence or reasoning
check.why: It is vague, has no support from the text, and does not explain anything.

check.q: In a theme paragraph, what is the job of reasoning?
choices: To explain how the evidence shows the theme
check.why: Reasoning is the bridge between the evidence and the claim.

check.q: Why should a theme paragraph mention the other side?
choices: Because it makes the paragraph longer
Because teachers require exactly four parts
Because it proves the theme is wrong
Because answering a fair objection makes the claim more trustworthy
check.why: Naming and answering a counterargument shows you have thought honestly about the text.

review.q: Which part of a plot shows the results of the climax playing out?
review.why: Falling action follows the climax and shows what it caused.

review.q: Why does a late climax usually make a story better?
choices: It gives tension time to build so the ending feels earned
It removes the need for a resolution
It lets readers skip the middle
review.why: Rising action needs room to close off easy choices and raise the stakes.

review.q: A story pauses to show what a character saw at the lake years earlier. This is:
review.why: A scene that jumps back in time to show an earlier event is a flashback.

review.q: Which is the best example of setting doing real work in a story?
choices: A story mentions it is Tuesday
A blizzard traps two enemies in one cabin so they must deal with each other
A character wears a red shirt
review.why: The setting creates the conflict by forcing the characters together.

review.q: Which statement is a theme, not a topic or a moral?
choices: Losing someone can teach a person what they still have
review.why: It is a full-sentence insight about life that does not depend on character names.

review.q: How does a theme develop over a whole novel?
choices: It is stated in the first sentence
Through repeated patterns, character change, and the ending
It does not; only fables have themes
review.why: Theme grows across the text and is confirmed by how the story ends.

review.q: What separates a symbol from an ordinary object in a story?
choices: Symbols are named in the title
Symbols repeat at key moments and stand for a larger idea, supported by evidence
review.why: A symbol must earn its meaning through repetition, placement, and characters' attention.

review.q: A film leaves out a novel's narrator's thoughts. What is the best way to discuss this?
choices: Explain what the change does to character and theme, and how the film tries to make up for it
Say the book is too long
Ignore it because films cannot show thoughts
review.why: A good comparison treats each change as a choice with effects, not as a mistake.
